verses.ar:
Name and title: Rabia bint Ismail al-Adawiyya al-Qaysiyya, of Basra, known as the saint of divine love.
Born: about 95–99 AH (about 714–717 CE), Basra; the sources vary.
Died: 185 AH (801 CE), Basra. One account places her death in Jerusalem.
Teachers: no teacher is recorded in the early sources. Later stories connect her with Hasan al-Basri, but scholars doubt them, as he died when she was a child.
Students: the ascetics and scholars who sought her out, among them Sufyan al-Thawri.
Works: none of her own. Her sayings and prayers were collected by later writers, above all by Farid al-Din Attar.

Rabia is said to have been born into a poor family in Basra, to have been orphaned and sold into slavery in a time of famine, and to have been freed by her master when he saw her devotion, after which she withdrew to a life of worship, fasting and prayer, first in the desert and later in her small house near Basra. Her life is known through stories set down long after her death, so the details cannot all be checked, but her place among the Sufis is firmly recorded from the earliest writers on the path. Scholars, ascetics and seekers came to sit with her, and she died in Basra in 185 AH, though some accounts place her death in Jerusalem.

Rabia is remembered above all for teaching that Allah is to be loved for Himself alone: not out of fear of the Fire and not out of hope for Paradise, which the sayings attributed to her call a veil between the lover and the One who made it. Britannica names her as the one who set out this ideal of selfless love for Allah, and Attar called her a second Maryam for her purity and singleness of heart. Her prayers, her tears and her tawakkul (trust in Allah) became a model for the Sufis who followed, and many of the sayings now ascribed to her may in fact belong to other women of the same name, so they should be read as part of the tradition rather than as her recorded words.
